Ladies and gentlemen, we are going to start. The 60th Plenary Meeting of the General Assembly is called to order. The Assembly will resume its consideration of Agenda Item 63 entitled Use of the veto. To hold a debate pursuant to Resolution 76/262 of 26 April 2022 on the situation as to which the veto was cast by a permanent member at the 9866th Meeting of the Security Council on 24th February 2025 under the agenda item entitled Maintenance of Peace and Security of Ukraine. In connection with this debate, the Assembly has before it a special report of the Security Council circulated in document A/7979/24. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, we meet once again pursuant to General Assembly Resolution 76/262, also known as the Veto Initiative. Following the casting of a veto by a permanent member of the Security Council. It is regrettable that we must convene under these circumstances, as the frequency of vetoes has continued to rise since 2022. Today's meeting serves as yet another reminder That while the Security Council bears primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security, the General Assembly plays a crucial role in responding to conflicts and crises. The efforts of both must be complementary, reinforcing one another in the pursuit of peace. In this regard, I welcome the timely submission of the Security Council Special Report on the Use of the Veto on 28 February this year. The veto initiative clearly demonstrates an improvement in the United Nations' capacity to address matters of international security. But we could do more. We could reflect on how the outcomes of deliberations on the veto initiative can be more binding. Excellencies, the General Assembly must remain steadfast in promoting peaceful solutions and inclusive dialogue. At the plenary meeting of the 11th Emergency Special Session on 24 February 2025, the General Assembly adopted 2 resolutions, one entitled Advancing a Comprehensive, Just and Lasting Peace in Ukraine, and the other entitled The Path to Peace. In both resolutions, the General Assembly reaffirmed its unwavering commitment to the sovereignty, independence, unity, and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders. Moreover, the Assembly has unequivocal— the Assembly was unequivocal in its call for a just, lasting, and comprehensive peace between Ukraine and the Russian Federation, a peace that aligns with the Charter of the United Nations and the principles of sovereign equality and territorial integrity. I call upon member states to actively work toward the implementation of these resolutions and to reaffirm their commitment to upholding the United Nations Charter and international law. Let us meet this responsibility with urgency and resolve to make a just and lasting peace a reality. I thank you. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation.

In the spirit of the Copenhagen and Bergenstock ultimatum, which would not only help find peace to this conflict, and on the other hand, it would hinder peace. Respect for territorial integrity of states, of course, that's a fundamental principle, but it can't be looked at in isolation from the right of nations to self-determination and the respect for human rights. Indeed, it's the Kiev regime's non-compliance with the last 2 of these principles, which are also contained in the UN Charter, which was one of the root causes of the Ukraine conflict. The regime that came to power in 2014 as a result of an anti-constitutional state coup directed and sponsored by the West immediately rolled out a war against its own citizens who had stood up to defend their rights and their identity for the Russian speakers of the Donbas on fabricated grounds of— on the fabricated grounds of the fight against terrorism. All of this with the complete silence of international organizations and with the encouragement of the West. Russia was forced to start its special military operation 3 years ago to stop this massacre and did it only when, when all diplomatic methods, including the Minsk agreements trampled on by the Kiev regime, had been exhausted. Colleagues, don't be fooled. In proposing these amendments that skewed the essence of the American text, the Europeans were trying to force you members of the Security Council to sign up to this manipulation of ideas that they're putting forward. It's also clear today all efforts of a large number of countries in Europe are focused only on making sure any realistic initiatives to find a solution to the Ukrainian conflict reach a dead end. They even fund it. In its best Orwellian traditions, including from the European Peace Fund, there's no doubt that the 24th of February attempt to skew the American text with politicized, unbalanced passages is nothing other than a clear obstruction to what we've seen as positive steps on the peace track. The fact that the Kyiv regime and the European capitals that support their efforts are not trying to find peace, they're rather focused on continuing the war down to the last Ukrainian, it is clear in this for the military rhetoric that we've heard in recent weeks. Rather than looking for peace, they clearly stated that they need— Ukraine needs to fight for its geopolitical— therefore their geopolitical interests. And the Kyiv prince could further forcibly cast hundreds of thousands of his own citizens into this senseless meat grinder. This, according to them, will help Kyiv have a strong negotiation position. However, the realistic— real situation on the front where this the Zelensky regime is irreversibly being defeated is clear as day. Hence the calls to continue to arm Ukraine, which, as we know, we've heard from different types of— from Macron, from Starmer, and others who are stoking this war. After this, we'll be able to hear from European representatives who clearly will demonstrate to you the level of degradation and Russophobia and hate to Russia from European diplomacy who are trying to provoke a new war on the Old Continent. Colleagues, we take a responsible attitude to the veto and would not have used it without serious and justifiable reasons. On the 24th of February, there was a choice between giving peace a chance or pushing it further away. Of course, we chose the first option. And this was why the UN founders came up with the veto. As discussion of questions of international peace and security shows, without this instrument, the Security Council would inevitably turn into a body which can only approve dubious, half-baked decisions produced by a conglomerate of Western countries which dominate the Security Council and ask and act on the basis of bloc discipline. In these conditions, only use of the veto will prevent decisions being taken which would not only weaken the authority of the Security Council, but also could damage international peace and security, worsen existing conflicts, and ultimately lead to even more suffering amongst civilians. Colleagues, let's not delude ourselves. The hawks that call for continuing of an armed conflict in Ukraine and in European countries are capitalizing on war and the suffering of civilians. And they don't plan on dropping their intent— intention to interfere with peace between Russia and Ukraine. Let's call on all of those who are against this war to be alert to this and not allow the Kyiv regime's head honcho, who is no longer legitimate, as well as the European allies, to torpedo constructive starts between Russia and the US, however beautifully Brussels, Paris, Berlin, and London dress up their new destructive ideas. Thank you. Thank you for your attention.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Estonia, who will speak on behalf of the Baltic countries.

President, I'm delivering this statement on behalf of the Baltic States— Latvia, Lithuania, and my own country, Estonia. We align ourselves with the statements to be delivered by the European Union and Liechtenstein on behalf of a group of countries. President, At the UN Security Council meeting on 24th of February, Russia used its veto power against 2 separate amendments to a UN Security Council Resolution 2774 tabled by the United States. The amendments proposed by a group of European countries— Denmark, France, Greece, Slovenia, and the United Kingdom— were intended to reaffirm the UN Security Council's commitment to reach a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in line with the UN Charter. These proposals were respectively supported by 9 and 11 members of the UN Security Council. And yet, Russia decided to ignore the position of a majority of the Security Council members by voting against these principled amendments. Russia's vetoes also totally ignored the expression of the political will of the most democratic body of the UN, this very UN General Assembly, which on the same morning gave its overwhelming support to 2 resolutions calling for a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine based on the UN Charter. By participating in the UN Security Council voting, Russia, as a party who unleashed the aggression, clearly violated Article 27 of the UN Charter. We also note that with the adoption of this resolution, UN Security Council has for the first time officially acknowledged Russia as a party in this war. At the UN Security Council, Russia stated that it considers a reference to the UN Charter as a disruption to a peace process. rather than a fundamental basis for a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace. Let me remind that the main purpose of the UN Charter is to maintain international peace and security. Baltic States condemn another abuse of the veto right by Russia. This undermines the principles of the UN Charter and is not compatible with Russia's obligations as a permanent member of the UN Security Council. President, to make it clear again that Russia is the aggressor and Ukraine is the victim of the aggression. Russia has no real desire for peace in Ukraine, otherwise they would have stopped the war of aggression and bloodshed a long time ago. Even now, instead of adhering to the resolution it supported and, I quote, swiftly ending the conflict, End of quote. Russia has continued the aggression by sending additional cannon fodder to Ukraine and by launching barrage of drones and glide bombs towards Ukraine every single day. Common sense suggests that the simplest and quickest way to end this war is not by appeasing the Kremlin's dictator, but through a full and immediate withdrawal of Russian troops from the territory of Ukraine. within its internationally recognized borders, extending also to its territorial waters. Finally, impunity for the crime of aggression undermines international legal order and would only lead to new crimes. We cannot tolerate this. Therefore, Russia must face full international accountability for its deeds. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Estonia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Iceland, who will speak on behalf of the Nordic countries.

Thank you, Mr. President. President, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the 5 Nordic countries: Denmark, Finland, Norway, Sweden, and my own country, Iceland. I would like to thank you for convening this debate under General Assembly Resolution 76262. We welcome the special report submitted by the Security Council on the use of the veto, in this case twice, At the 9866th meeting of the Council on February 24th. President, the Security Council has primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security. In carrying out its duties under this responsibility, the Council acts on behalf of the general membership. During the resumed emergency session on Ukraine on February 24th, the General Assembly adopted 2 resolutions on Ukraine: Advancing a Comprehensive, Just, and Lasting Peace in Ukraine and The Path to Peace, with a clear 2/3 majority. Both resolutions underline the commitment to key principles in the UN Charter in bringing about peace for Ukraine that includes respect for its sovereignty, independence, unity, and territorial integrity. within its internationally recognized borders. Both resolutions recognized that there can be no equivalence between how we refer to Ukraine and to the Russian Federation in the ongoing war. The first is the victim, the second the aggressor. No one wants peace more than Ukraine and its people. No one feels the effects of the war more than them. For peace to be lasting, it must be in accordance with international law, including the rules and principles of the UN Charter. Russia and other potential aggressors must not draw the conclusion that violations of international law will pass without consequences. That would risk renewed aggression and undermine global security. The resolution, The Path to Peace, as amended and then adopted by the General Assembly reflects that determination of the general membership to uphold the principles and obligations of the UN Charter, which we have all committed to uphold. It also reflects members' clear-eyed view of who attacked whom. The resolution adopted by the General Assembly calls for a swift end to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine by the Russian Federation, but rejects the precept that an invasion of any country is in any way acceptable. It mourns the tragic loss of life, including thousands of civilian lives, and rejects the precept that one country can simply change by force the borders of another and occupy and annex its territories. We underline that this constitutes a violation of international law and that accountability must be ensured. The resolution, The Path to Peace, as adopted by the Security Council, does not reflect these core principles. It does not give an accurate picture of how we have come to this point. Despite proposals for amendments to reflect the wishes of the General Membership on respecting the core principles of the Charter, the Russian Federation exercised its veto twice. Russia vetoed amendments calling for a just, lasting, and comprehensive peace in line with the UN Charter. President, it is unacceptable that a permanent member of the Security Council should oppose language supporting the central rules of the Charter. Article 27, Part 3 of the UN Charter sets out one limitation on voting, including to those— to the use of the veto. To quote the Charter, in decisions under Chapter VI and under paragraph 3 of Article 52, a party to a dispute shall abstain from voting. We reiterate our call for the veto to be used responsibly and only in strict adherence with the Charter. We believe that for the Security Council to live up to its obligations and to recoup the respect many feel it has forfeited, Permanent members cannot allow themselves to use the veto in a patently partisan manner. And the Security Council cannot allow itself to be seen to disregard the clear wishes of the entire membership of the United Nations, expressed through the General Assembly. We regret that on Monday last week, the Council allowed the self-interest of the aggressor state to trample over the legitimate views and aspirations of the broader membership. Let me conclude by once again affirming the steadfast and unwavering support of the 5 Nordic countries for Ukraine and its people. And may I add, a commitment that was also resoundingly reaffirmed by a vast majority of the world's countries last week. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Iceland. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Luxembourg who will speak on behalf of the Benelux countries.

President, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Benelux countries: Belgium, the Kingdom of the Netherlands, and my own country, Luxembourg. We fully subscribe to the statements made by the European Union as well as by Liechtenstein on behalf of a group of countries. Benelux countries would like to thank you, President, for convening this debate in accordance with Resolution 76/262 in application of the veto initiative spearheaded by Liechtenstein. An important impetus for The adoption of Resolution 76262 was the widespread concerns amongst members of this Assembly over the Security Council's paralysis in the face of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, a sovereign member state of the United Nations. As we meet, Russian forces continue to intensify their attacks on the civilian population and civilian infrastructure in Ukraine. Ukraine in violation of international humanitarian law. On the 24th of February, the General Assembly adopted 2 resolutions in which it reiterated the need to redouble diplomatic efforts to achieve a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine in line with the Charter of the United Nations and its principles of the sovereign equality and territorial integrity of states. To quote our colleague, the Permanent Representative of France, in adopting these resolutions, the General Assembly has been the moral compass of this organization, the guarantor of a rules-based international order and of the sovereign equality of states. By contrast, Russia abused its veto power in the Security Council by voting against territorial integrity and peace in line with the UN Charter. Benelux countries remain steadfast in defending the principles of international law and the UN Charter in all situations, whether that be in the Middle East, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sudan, Myanmar or Ukraine. Our position is clear: safeguarding the integrity of the international system requires the same commitment to justice and accountability in all crises. After 3 years of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Resolution 2774 adopted by the Security Council on the 24th of February makes no reference to the party that is responsible for this invasion— Russia. It makes no reference to the sovereignty, independence, unity, and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders extending to its territorial waters. And it makes no reference to the need for peace between Ukraine and the Russian Federation to be not just lasting but also just and comprehensive and in line with the UN Charter and the principles of sovereign equality and territorial integrity of states. It was precisely to correct those glaring omissions and to bring the resolution in line with the resolutions adopted by the General Assembly a few hours earlier that the European members of the Security Council— Denmark, France, Greece, Slovenia, and the United Kingdom— presented amendments to the draft resolution submitted by the United States of America. We deeply regret that 2 amendments which enjoyed broad support among Council members were not adopted due to the use of the veto by Russia. The fact that Russia portrayed the amendments referencing the Charter and its principles as being, and I quote, unbalanced, politicised, and an act of sabotage, is not acceptable for the vast majority of member states that are truly committed to respecting the Charter. What is also not acceptable is that we have again witnessed a situation where the perpetrator acts as the judge in his own case. All members of the Security Council must adhere to Article 27, paragraph 3 of the Charter, which states that, and I quote, a party to a dispute shall abstain from voting. In the Pact for the Future and Action 41, we've all decided to implement this provision. If any lack of clarity on the scope or definition of this clause is the reason this Charter obligation has not been honoured in full, then it must be addressed as a matter of priority. The Benelux countries welcome efforts to end the war in Ukraine through diplomacy and dialogue. As long as those efforts are based on the principles of the UN Charter, including the principles of sovereign equality and territorial integrity of states. Peace in Ukraine will only be sustainable if it is just and if it is underpinned by strong and credible security guarantees. In its just and courageous fight to defend its freedom and our common universal values, Ukraine can continue to count on the full support and solidarity of the Benelux countries. We will continue to resolutely support the independence, unity, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders. Thank you very much.

Thank you, Mr. President. I have the honor to take the floor this morning on behalf of the following group of states: Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Canada, Costa Rica, Croatia, Cyprus, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Iceland, Italy, Ireland, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, Kingdom of the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Republic of Moldova, Romania, Singapore, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Ukraine, and my own country, Liechtenstein. We thank you for convening this Assembly in a timely manner after the casting of vetoes by the Russian Federation on 2 amendments to a draft adopted subsequently as Resolution 2774. We appreciate the production of a special report by the Council and the presence of the vetoing state at today's meeting, both of which are in line with the provisions of Resolution 76262, otherwise known as the veto initiative. We look forward to receiving a summary of today's meeting to be sent to the Security Council for their reflection. Mr. President, the vetoes we discuss today and the resolution they attained to were concerning in their own right. To adopt a text that does not acknowledge the manifest violation of the UN Charter by the Russian Federation through its aggression against Ukraine, nor Ukraine's sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity, sets a concerning precedent for the security of each and every member state represented here today. The Charter is impartial, but it is always on the side of international law. It is on the side of territorial integrity, sovereign equality, and against the illegal use of force. The amendments brought by European members of the Council which reflected these facts would have contributed to bringing the text into line with the Charter. But today we must also address the constitutional implications of the resolution adopted in the Council. The Security Council, after it was prevented from exercising its primary responsibility for the maintenance of peace and security, delegated its responsibility for the situation in Ukraine to the General Assembly in its Resolution 2623. 23rd of 2022. This Assembly, discharging that responsibility, proceeded to adopt 2 resolutions on the morning of February 24th, which made it very clear what the position of the membership was. That the Council should then proceed to adopt a text so clearly failing to meet the standards set out by the membership Mr. President, the further aspect of the Council's resolution also requires consideration. The draft resolution adopted in the Council set out that the, and I quote, principal purpose, end of quote, of the United Nations is to maintain international peace and security and peacefully settle disputes, and separately named the parties to the conflict as the Russian Federation and and Ukraine. The resolution therefore clearly infers that the Russian Federation is a party to a dispute germane to the resolution. Article 27, Part III of the UN Charter sets out one limitation on voting, including to the use of the veto. And I quote, provided that in decisions under Chapter VI and under Para. of Article 52, a party to a dispute shall abstain from voting. The Russian Federation should therefore have abstained from voting on Resolution 2724. Mr. President, let us not forget, the Russian Federation is violating the Charter in exercising its veto in respect of the situation in Ukraine. Members of the Council raised the issue that Russia was a party to a dispute in February 2022 when it vetoed Council action addressing its aggression against Ukraine. And in September last year, all of our leaders collectively adopted a Pact for the Future in which we decided to, and I quote, fully implement and adhere to all provisions of the Charter of the United Nations as they relate to the decision-making process in the Security Council, including Article 27 of the Charter. End of quote. We must stand up against this grave abuse of the Charter, which compounds the already flagrant violation of Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty. And we look forward to working with all interested parties to enhance the implementation of this provision at a time when it is so badly needed. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Liechtenstein. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Austria.

Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, Excellencies, Austria aligns itself with the statement of the European Union representative to be delivered and the statement just now delivered by the distinguished representative of Liechtenstein with a view to the implementation of Article 27 of the Charter. Last week, Russia exercised its veto in the Security Council on 2 amendments on a resolution regarding Ukraine, one of them reaffirming the commitment to sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of Ukraine, and another one urging a just, lasting and comprehensive peace between Ukraine and Russia. These amendments would have served to reflect the position of the majority of member states voting in this General Assembly just hours before. Members of the Security Council, and especially the permanent ones, serve on behalf of all of us. They were conferred a special responsibility through the UN Charter It is therefore highly regrettable that this responsibility was not used the way it had been intended. Excellencies, this is why today the UN General Assembly has the opportunity to reiterate its positions. In addition to our debate during the 11th Emergency Special Session last week, today we reiterate our expectation that the core principles of the the UN Charter and international law are adhered to anywhere and at all times. Let me therefore repeat 3 points. First, we condemn Russia's unprovoked, unjustified, and illegal full-scale aggression against its neighbor Ukraine. Second, this represents a clear violation of international law. And third, no negotiation about Ukraine without Ukraine. No decisions on European security without Europe. And in response to the Russian statement just before, of course we stand for peace, a just, lasting, and comprehensive peace. More than 2/3 of UN member states have signed the Code of Conduct on the Use of the Veto launched by the Accountability Coherence and Transparency Group, of which Austria is an active member. In addition, the Pact for the Future took up the key provision from the ACT Code of Conduct in its Action 41B and therefore universalized it. We therefore encourage all member states, all member states, including those permanent members of the Council who have not done so, to support this initiative. The veto initiative in the General Assembly has contributed to the accountability and transparency of the Security Council towards the wider membership. It has given a boost to the General Assembly to fill the void created by the Security Council with regard to the maintenance of international peace and security. Mr. President, now we as the General Assembly must ensure that we insist on the adherence to these principles and norms of the Charter. This is important for all our states. Territorial integrity, peaceful settlement of disputes, disputes, and the non-use of force are key examples of the universally binding principles we all agreed to. And for the majority of the member states in this room, they serve as an important pillar of our security policy itself. Austria, for example, is a neutral state who is not part of any military alliance. The adherence to international law and cooperation in multilateral fora is therefore part of our DNA. This is why Austria will continue to insist that these principles and laws are upheld in the General Assembly, as well as if elected as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council in the years 2027 and '28. I today ensure you that Austria will continue to be a reliable partner and do its best to ensure that our Charter is preserved. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

I thank the distinguished representative of Austria. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the European Union who shall speak on behalf of the European Union and its member states.

Mr. President, colleagues, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the European Union. The candidate countries Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Georgia, as well as Andorra, Monaco, and San Marino, align themselves with this statement. I want to thank the President of the General Assembly for convening this meeting. We are here today because of Russia's decision to twice veto amendments to UN Security Council Resolution 2774 on peace in Ukraine, amendments that were proposed by the European members of the Security Council. The first veto blocked a reference to the Security Council's commitment to the sovereignty, independence, unity, and territorial integrity of Ukraine. This amendment received 9 positive votes. The second Russian veto obstructed a call for a just, lasting and comprehensive peace in line with the UN Charter. This proposal received 11 positive votes. Let it be clear: Russia is abusing its veto power to block references to the principle of territorial integrity and to peace in line with the UN Charter. For over 3 years now, it has bombed Ukraine's cities on a daily basis as part of its unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression. And it is abusing its privileged position at the UN to avoid being called out. The UN membership cannot allow such behavior to pass. Russia is undermining the core principles of our multilateral system, and aggression is an aggression, wherever it occurs. We cannot accept an equivalence between the aggressor and the victim of aggression. We cannot accept a world where might is right. Where the power of law is replaced by the power of guns. We believe in a world based on rules. The time for peace is now. The EU supports all meaningful efforts to bring an end to Russia's war of aggression. International law, including the UN Charter, must be the reference point for any peace in Ukraine or elsewhere. In 2 resolutions adopted last Monday with overwhelming majorities, this UN General Assembly called for a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine based on the UN Charter. We would like to extend our sincere appreciation to all member states who supported the resolution entitled Advancing a Comprehensive, Just, and Lasting Peace in Ukraine. It was an important step to highlight the necessity of the rule of law as well as the global consequences of Russia's aggression. The General Assembly has called for an end to the war this year. By vetoing constructive amendments to a resolution on Europe's proposed by the European members of the Security Council, Russia is obstructing the path to peace. It's ignoring what was decided by the General Assembly. No one wants peace and needs peace in Ukraine more than the Ukrainian people. No one has a larger stake in European security than Europeans. And no one can afford to ignore the devastating consequences consequences of this war for regional and global stability. The EU will continue to work with all our partners on a just, lasting, and comprehensive peace that ensures Ukraine's future sovereignty and security. Mr. President, a peace that rewards the aggressor increases the risk for any country to face similar aggression. A peace in line with the Charter however, ensures a safer world for all of us. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the European Union. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Australia, who will speak on behalf of Canada, Australia, and New Zealand.

Thank you, President, for convening this meeting. I deliver this statement on behalf of Canada, New Zealand, and my own country, Australia. We are here today to discuss Russia's use of the veto pursuant to the Veto Initiative, which is a vital mechanism for promoting greater transparency and accountability of the UN Security Council. The United States resolution, The Path to Peace, is the only resolution on Ukraine adopted by the Security Council since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It was adopted despite Russia's veto of amendments referring to key elements of the UN Charter, namely sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity, as well as the need for a just, comprehensive, and lasting peace in Ukraine. President, on the 3rd anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the General Assembly reaffirmed its respect for the UN Charter, and for Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity. In addition to causing terrible loss of life and damage in Ukraine, Russia's war is compounding human suffering and the crisis in food and energy security globally. Russia's aggression has serious implications for security in both the Euro-Atlantic and the Indo-Pacific, as demonstrated by the deeply concerning military cooperation between Russia and the DPRK, Including troop deployments to Russia for combat against Ukraine. The DPRK's export of ballistic missiles, artillery shells, and other military materiel to Russia for use against Ukraine, and Russia's training of DPRK troops involving arms or related materiel, represents flagrant violations of UN Security Council resolutions. President, Last Monday, while other members expressed their unwavering commitment to the core Charter principles of sovereign equality and territorial integrity of states, Russia vetoed it. What principle of international law did it call upon states to follow instead? None. Instead, it asked member states to recognise a new reality it had imposed on the ground by force. The message from this permanent member of the Security Council to any leader with a vulnerable border is clear. CANZ countries reject Russia's message. We believe that all countries are better off in a world where international rules are clear, mutually agreed, and consistently followed. We condemn Russia's illegal and immoral invasion of Ukraine and fully support all meaningful progress towards a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace which preserves Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity, supports security and stability in Europe, and ensures Russia does not renew its aggression. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Australia. And I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Portugal.

Thank you, Mr. President. Portugal aligns itself with the statements delivered by the European Union and by Liechtenstein on behalf of a group of countries. As a co-sponsor of the veto initiative, Portugal deeply regrets the use of the veto against 2 different amendments aimed at upholding fundamental principles of the UN Charter, namely those of sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity. Russia's vetoes on February 24th reflect its unwillingness to abide by the principles of justice and international law that constitute the very foundation of this organization. And that guide respectful relations among equally sovereign states. The amendments in question had already been adopted by this General Assembly and would have thus translated this membership's collective will, which was, as such, procrastinated by one single member. Such actions undermine multilateralism and weaken the credibility of the United Nations. Furthermore, Article 27 of the UN Charter is clear: a party to a dispute must abstain from voting. Russia, as a party to the war against Ukraine, should have refrained from casting its vote. Yet it continues to act as both judge and jury, shielding itself from accountability while violating the fundamental principles that this organization was created to uphold. It is imperative that the Security Council enforces Article 27 and that the General Assembly ensures that its resolutions are not circumvented by unilateral obstruction. UN Charter principles are not selective. They cannot be cherry-picked according to one's national interests. They are a collective threshold of our global community and must be addressed in their entirety without ambiguities, and in all contexts and all regions. That is the only way to ensure equal treatment of nations, large and small, and to preserve international peace and security. Because we all want peace, but not any peace, not at any cost. We want, and we need, a peace firmly anchored in the UN Charter, a peace that is reached through strict adherence to the rules of international law, including international humanitarian law. A peace that doesn't reward the aggressor nor sets a dangerous precedent for future violations of territorial integrity or political independence of any state. A peace that lastingly ends the immense human suffering and massive damage to infrastructure by ensuring accountability of the culprits. A peace that will ensure long-term security security and stability of the European continent through a comprehensive framework negotiated with all relevant actors. Mr. President, we stress the importance of the accountability for the use of the veto in the Security Council. Its use must be restricted, exercised sensibly, and in strict adherence to the Charter until a consensus is reached to abolish it. Despite this setback, we remain hopeful that the international community's unwavering support to the Ukrainian people will create new opportunities for the United Nations to contribute to a just, lasting, and comprehensive peace in the country according to the collective political will widely reflected in this General Assembly's resolutions adopted on February 24th. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Portugal, and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom.

Mr. President, last week this Assembly marked 3 years since Russia's unprovoked invasion of Ukraine. in flagrant violation of the UN Charter. This Assembly voted decisively in support of Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity and of the UN Charter based on the facts. This was an invasion of a sovereign country by its neighbor. It was a war of choice. As my Prime Minister has made clear, the UK continues to support peace in Ukraine. Our approach is based on 4 principles. First, to support Ukraine's legitimate right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter. Second, any lasting peace must guarantee the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine, and Ukraine must be at the negotiating table. Third and fourth, when a peace deal is reached, as a European neighbor, we will continue to support Ukraine's defense and deterrence capability. And we are ready to develop a coalition of the willing to defend a peace deal in Ukraine. For peace to be sustainable, it must be strong and just and deter further Russian aggression against its neighbours. This is why the UK, along with other Security Council members, proposed amendments that would bring the Security Council resolution in line with the resolutions of the General Assembly, which had been adopted just hours beforehand. These amendments sought to acknowledge Russia as the perpetrator of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, to reaffirm our commitment to the territorial integrity of Ukraine, and to ensure that peace in Ukraine would be in line with the UN Charter. In order to stop us, Russia exercised its veto. In doing so, it flouted the voice of the General Assembly. It vetoed respect for the UN Charter and for the sovereignty of a neighbor. And all the while, Russia has continued its campaign of aggression against Ukraine, including with this week's drone attacks on civilian buildings in Kharkiv. We should judge Putin by his actions, and these are not the actions of a peacemaker. As we sit here today discussing Russia's use of the veto on amendments regarding its own violations of the UN Charter, let us remember one thing. If Putin wanted peace, he could have it tomorrow. All Russia needs to do is cease its aggression and withdraw withdraw its forces from all of Ukraine. I thank you, President.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Switzerland.

Mr. President, Switzerland aligns itself with the statement made by Liechtenstein, and we're grateful for convening this meeting. Last week, as we commemorated Russia's military aggression against Ukraine for the 3rd year, the Security Council adopted its first resolution Addressing the matter. Switzerland deeply regrets that 2 essential amendments were vetoed. These amendments contain fundamental references to the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations. The omissions in Resolution 2774 are all the more striking when compared to the resolutions adopted on the same day by the General Assembly. This divergence between these 2 principal organs of the United Nations highlights the relevance of today's debate. Switzerland constantly advocates for a responsible and moderate use of the right of veto. The present case leads us to reaffirm Switzerland's support for the principle that Council members Who are parties to a dispute have an obligation to abstain from voting under Chapter VI of the Charter, as stipulated in Article 27. The reasoning behind this principle, which is also explicitly mentioned in the Pact for the Future, is simple: no one should be the judge of their own cause. Respect for this principle is essential to preserving the legitimacy of the Council Russia has disregarded the obligation to refrain from using its veto, provided for in Article 27 of the Charter, in a war it is waging in violation of the same Charter. Once again, we find ourselves in a situation where one violation of the Charter feeds another, as this resolution clearly falls under Chapter VI of the Charter. The party to the conflict, which is also mentioned in the text of the resolution, should not only have refrained from vetoing the amendments, but also from voting on the resolution itself. Mr. President, after more than 3 years of immense suffering caused by the devastating war against Ukraine, we welcome the Security Council's willingness to advance peace. However, As Switzerland has stated on several occasions, both during our term on the Council and before the General Assembly, this peace must be based on international law, including the United Nations Charter. Like the vast majority of member states, we support Ukraine's sovereignty, independence, unity, and territorial integrity. Switzerland is also committed to a just, lasting, and comprehensive peace, in accordance with the United Nations Charter, which the General Assembly reaffirmed once again just a few hours before the Council's vote. The vetoes in the Council which blocked precisely those elements were thus not only at odds with the will of the majority of the Council members, but also with the clear clear will of the General Assembly. We therefore consider that the resolutions adopted by the General Assembly constitute the point of reference and clearly express the expectations of Member States. We ask the Security Council to fully take them into account, in accordance with Article 24 of the Charter, and expect it to do so for a peace that respects the fundamental purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Switzerland and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Bulgaria.

Mr. President, Bulgaria aligns itself with the statements delivered by the European Union and by Liechtenstein on behalf of a group of states committed to the implementation of Resolution 76/262. I would like to highlight a few points in my national capacity. We're gathered here today because of the Russian Federation's decision to veto 2 amendments reaffirming the principles of the UN Charter and the parameters of a just peace, amendments that the General Assembly had clearly endorsed just just hours earlier. The Assembly spoke in favor of a just and lasting peace, one rooted in the UN Charter and the principles of sovereign equality and territorial integrity. Yet the Russian Federation chose to disregard the will of the Assembly, abusing its veto power to serve its own interests. In doing so, it violated Article 24 of the UN Charter, which stipulates that Security Council members act on behalf of all member states. Furthermore, Russia's veto contradicts Article 27 of the Charter, which requires a party to a dispute to abstain from voting. The Russian Federation is undeniably a party to this dispute, as acknowledged even in the Security Council resolution it supported on February 24th. Thank you. 2024. For 3 years, the Russian Federation has waged an illegal, unprovoked, and utterly unjustified full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine, a blatant violation of international law, the UN Charter, and the fundamental principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity. If we are to achieve a just and lasting peace, aggression must not be rewarded. There can be no moral or legal equivalence between the aggressor and the victim. The Security Council must be unequivocal in this stance, especially when the General Assembly has already made its position clear. For 3 years, this Assembly and the Secretary-General have demonstrated unwavering commitment to a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine. A peace based on the UN Charter and international law, a peace that upholds Ukraine's sovereignty, territorial integrity, and independence, and a peace that, that does not demand the surrender of the state that was attacked. By vetoing these amendments, Russia is attempting to rewrite the history of its illegal invasion, undermine the UN Charter as the foundation of international order and reduce accountability for the atrocities committed in Ukraine to nothing more than an empty promise. Bulgaria remains committed to peace in Ukraine. However, any discussion of peace must be firmly grounded in international law and the UN Charter. No peace initiative or negotiation framework should proceed without Ukraine's direct involvement. Moreover, Ukraine must enter any negotiations from the strongest possible position. The foundation of any future peace must include full accountability for Russia's crimes in Ukraine. We must all stand up for the UN Charter, for upholding its principles is an investment in and guarantee for both global and national security. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Bulgaria and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Romania.

Mr. President, Romania joins the statement of the European Union and also the statement delivered by Liechtenstein on behalf of a group of countries. In this hall last week, we debated and voted on bringing peace in Ukraine based on the UN Charter, 3 years after the start of the full-scale Russian invasion. And the General Assembly has pronounced itself in a straightforward and forward-looking manner on the need to reach a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine. On the same day, the Security Council also considered the future peace in Ukraine, and we sincerely thank the European members of the Security Council, that tried to bring Resolution 2774 in line with the text adopted by the General Assembly earlier that day. Our appreciation also goes to those members of the Council that either supported or at least did not object to those amendments during the vote. Regrettably, the Russian Federation decided to use its veto power against the 2 amendments in the Security Council. Its isolated voice in the General Assembly has been echoed in the Council, where the rules differ, and Russia stood alone as well. And our analysis is crystal clear. The 2 vetoes in the Security Council cast by Russia represent a veto against the UN Charter. Russia vetoed the principles of sovereign equality and the territorial integrity of states. This should raise in itself the alarm for every single member of the United Nations. The 2 vetoes are also blatant disregard of the strong message of the most representative body of the United Nations, namely the General Assembly, which defined very clearly only a couple of hours earlier the parameters for achieving a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine. We regret to see a Council that once again acts with disregard to the clear guidance of the international community. Mr. President, the General Assembly is reunited today to reconfirm that a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine can only be achieved if it is rooted in the UN Charter. A capitulation in front of the aggressor state will never lead to peace. And the General Assembly has proved time and again that it is not afraid to use the correct qualification of the war. This is a textbook example of an unjustified and illegal act of aggression against Ukraine. And we will repeat it today, just as we have done it for the past almost— more than, actually, 36 months since the full-scale aggression started. First, we need a peace that looks indeed at the root cause: the blatant attack on a neighboring country in violation of the prohibition of the use of force. We need a peace that brings to the table first and foremost Ukraine, as well as all interested parties and European countries, which are one of those interested in having peace but not under any circumstances. And we need a peace that takes into account the suffering of all civilians affected by indiscriminate rocket and drone attacks and who sought shelter in other countries. Mr. President, before I conclude, allow me to reconfirm that my delegation is one of a long list of countries that supports the full implementation of Article 27, Para 3 of the UN Charter, which sets out a limitation on voting in the Council, which provides that, quote, a party to a dispute shall abstain from voting, unquote. And Russia might continue selectively to interpret the Charter, but this is not its prerogative. The UN Charter needs to be respected in its entirety, and we expect the Security Council to fulfill this duty since it acts on behalf of the entire UN membership. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of Romania and now call upon the distinguished representative of Malta to take the floor.

Thank you. Thank you, President. Malta aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union and also the statement by Liechtenstein on behalf of a group of states and would like to make additional remarks in its national capacity. Malta regrets the use of the veto on 2 amendments to a resolution that would have first sought to reaffirm the principle of sovereignty and territorial integrity of States by prohibiting the threat and use of force. This is not only a principle under the UN Charter but also a principle recognized as customary international law. Secondly, it would have called for a just, lasting, and comprehensive peace in line with the UN Charter. Such a peace will ultimately safeguard the security interests of Ukraine and its people. in full respect of principles of sovereignty, sovereign equality, and territorial integrity of states, and under— as underlined in various UN resolutions. The consequences of this war have been tragic for Ukraine and its people. The time has come for this war to stop. Malta remains firm in calling on Russia to immediately cease all hostilities and to unconditionally and completely withdraw all its forces and military equipment from the entire territory of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders. Malta also stands united with those who strive to uphold universal principles enshrined in the United Nations Charter and to advance the implementation of the resolutions adopted by the General Assembly. In 2 resolutions adopted last Monday in this very hall, the UN General Assembly called for a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine based on the UN Charter. The GA has called for an end to the war this year. By vetoing constructive amendments to resolutions on Europe's security, the General Assembly is being ignored. In closing, we believe that a just, lasting, and comprehensive peace in Ukraine requires the immediate end of hostilities by Russia, together with the unconditional and full withdrawal of Russian military forces from Ukraine's entire territory in its internationally recognized borders. In this spirit, Malta will continue to support all efforts aimed at finding solutions to address the consequences
I thank the distinguished representatives— representative of Malta, and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the United States.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Thank you, Mr. President. The action in the Security Council on February 24th demonstrated that the United States is committed to ending the Russia-Ukraine war. Hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians and Russians have died. The longer the war continues, the greater the suffering for both nations. The war must end now, and the peace must be durable and lasting. lasting, not a temporary pause. With the adoption of Resolution 2774, the Security Council showed that the United Nations can still live up to the purposes and principles of its Charter, mainly to maintain international peace and security, including through the peaceful settlement of disputes. We reminded the world that there is common ground that we can all agree on. All UN member states can agree that the war is a tragedy and that it must end. Security Council Resolution 2774 does not end the war, but it has put us on a path to peace. The United States is fully committed to playing a meaningful and constructive role in the pursuit of peace. Mr. President, The Security Council has proven that the UN is committed to and capable of helping to accomplish its original purpose. We look forward to continued work in this regard. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the United States and now call upon the distinguished representative of Italy. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of

Thank you, Mr. President. Last week, on the 3rd anniversary of Russia's illegal invasion of Ukraine, the Security Council adopted its first resolution on this matter. The resolution emphasized the international community's aspiration for the swift end of the war, while also urging lasting peace between Ukraine and Russia. The Republic of Korea believes there are 2 goals that everyone can agree on. One, this senseless An unlawful war must come to an end as soon as possible. And 2, we must strive to uphold the fundamental principles of the UN Charter and international law. This war of aggression against a sovereign state continues to shake the structural foundations of the international order and the rules and norms that underpin it. In this light, the Republic of Korea voted in favor of the amendments that were proposed by the 5 European countries of the Council, which explicitly stated the guiding principles of the UN Charter. In line with, in line with the proposed amendments, My delegation is of the view that Russia's invasion of Ukraine, sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of Ukraine, and the need for a just, lasting, and comprehensive peace based on the UN Charter were important elements to be included in a Security Council resolution on Ukraine. To support the resolution, considering the importance of garnering international support and determination for the swift end of the war in Ukraine. We should also remember that this war in Ukraine has inflicted unspeakable suffering and devastation for the past 3 years. Indeed, civilian casualties in Ukraine have surpassed 40,000, and more than 10 million people have been displaced, both internally and abroad. The tears of innocent civilians have long overflowed and are now nearly exhausted. Yet, the attacks on Ukraine have not been exhausted. In fact, they are even escalating over the past few weeks with large-scale drone and missile attacks on a plethora of Ukrainian cities. Mr. President, we hope that the adoption of the Security Council resolution will provide an opportunity for all relevant parties to further accelerate diplomatic efforts to achieve just, lasting, and comprehensive peace and stability in line with the UN Charter. The Republic of Korea will firmly support all these efforts and takes this opportunity to reaffirm our commitment to standing with the Ukrainian people as they preserve over the current hardship and rebuild their proud nations. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Republic of Korea. And I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Italy.

Mr. President, Italy fully aligns itself with the statements delivered by the European Union and Liechtenstein on behalf of a group of states and would like to add some considerations in its national capacity. Thank you. We are convened today to reaffirm our commitment to the UN Charter and to reiterate the need to ensure that the fundamental principles of international law prevail wherever they are challenged. The amendments proposed by the European Members of the Council on the Resolution Path to Peace reaffirmed the commitment of the international community to the sovereignty, independence, unity, and territorial integrity of Ukraine, and for a just, lasting and comprehensive peace between Ukraine and Russia, in line with the UN Charter. The same amendments, before being vetoed by Russia in the Council, had been approved by the 11th Emergency Special Session of the General Assembly, establishing essential tenets for the upcoming negotiations and for a future peace settlement. We firmly believe that the full implementation of these principles is a matter not only in the interests of Ukraine and Europe, but also of the entire UN membership, since they are the foundations that hold the international community together. We wish to recall that according to the 1970 Declaration of Principles of International Law concerning friendly relations among states, I quote, The territory of a state shall not be the object of acquisition by another state resulting from the threat or use of force. End quote. Unwavering support for independence and territorial integrity of Ukraine has been a priority for Italy since the beginning of the conflict. By strongly backing the European Union initiatives, Italy is contributing in particular to ensure Ukraine's resilience and intends to play an active role in the social and economic recovery of the country. We will host in July in Rome the Ukraine Recovery Conference. Together, we will lay the foundations for a prosperous, independent Ukraine within our common European family. As we have said many times, we are not at war with Russia, but we strongly uphold Ukraine's independence and territorial integrity. We are also concerned about the humanitarian crisis, the high toll of destruction, and the global consequences of the war. The only real way to alleviate people's suffering in Ukraine is to put an end to this war through negotiations leading to a just, verifiable, and monitored peace. We therefore encourage a diplomatic solution to the conflict based on the UN Charter, with the full involvement of Ukraine and Europe. Italy remains committed to collaborating with all partners ready to support peace efforts. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Italy. And I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Türkiye.

Mr. President, at the outset, I would like to express our appreciation for convening this debate in line with the General Assembly resolution 76/262, also known as the Veto Initiative. We are pleased to see that General Assembly resolutions continue to serve its purpose and remain a valuable tool on issues pertaining to international peace and security for the collective good of humanity. General Assembly debates enable the reflection of the collective political weight of the wider membership. They also offer further options of action to be explored whenever a veto is cast. Türkiye firmly believes that the use of veto is a serious setback to the founding principles of the UN and the Council's mandate to maintain international peace and security. The latest developments about Ukraine is a case in point, as the war has reached an inflection point and the focus has shifted from the battleground to the negotiations. Giving priority to diplomacy and negotiations instead of military methods is in line with the policy that Türkiye has pursued since the beginning of the war. We hope that this process will be the beginning of the end of the conflict and of the establishment of a lasting peace. A just and lasting peace cannot be achieved without the involvement of both parties. Given Türkiye's longstanding commitment to negotiations, we will remain in touch with both Russia and Ukraine to facilitate diplomatic talks. We discussed contributions that could be made by Türkiye on this important juncture, as well as Türkiye's desire to host the negotiations when President Zelenskyy was in Ankara. We also discussed our possible contributions, contributions to a diplomatic end to the war with Foreign Minister Lavrov, who visited Türkiye on 24th of February. Foreign Minister Fidan was in London last, last Sunday for the Leaders' Summit on Ukraine. We will keep remaining in touch with all sides to find a solution to this war. In fact, since the beginning of the conflict, our support for Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty remains steadfast. As Türkiye, we have voiced our strong support for a negotiated and diplomatic end to the conflict. We are one of the few countries that managed to maintain its dialogue with both Russia and Ukraine in the aftermath of the war, which enabled us to bring the conflicting parties together several times after the war started and to pioneer the Black Sea Initiative and various prisoner exchanges. Mr. President, on the 3rd anniversary of the war, we voted in favor of both resolutions submitted to the General Assembly. We consider these 2 develop— 2 resolutions complementary, as they both focus on Ukraine's territorial integrity as well as on a negotiated solution. At this critical juncture, we must focus on crafting a genuine solution rather than going after competing texts. We need a solution that originated from a strategic endgame, a solution that will be in the interest of not only our region but the whole world. Hence, as member states of the United Nations, we must contribute to establishment of a just and lasting peace as soon as possible. After achieving peace, we must all unite on devising the best way to preserve it. It is our sincere hope that it will be possible to reach a just and lasting end to this war through negotiations. We continue our strong commitment to Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty, independence, and keep the UN Charter at the heart of our efforts. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Türkiye, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Slovenia.

Thank you, Mr. President. Slovenia aligns itself with the EU statement, to which I will add some remarks in my national capacity. Mr. President, each veto is regrettable. To veto a reference to the UN Charter is absolutely deplorable. My country deeply regrets the, the 2 vetoes cast by the Russian Federation last week. With this, it single-handedly prevented the inclusion of references to the UN Charter and its principles in the Security Council's first resolution about the war on Ukraine. It furthermore also directly violated the Charter's limitations on the use of veto, namely Article 27, which instructs a party to a dispute to abstain from voting. Colleagues, for 3 years Russia is waging a war against Ukraine, in clear violation of the UN Charter and international law. And after 3 years of death and destruction, a just and lasting peace is long overdue. For this reason, we actively engaged in the process of the Council's consideration of the Path to Peace resolution. We respect the aim of the adopted resolution: to set in motion a path leading to peace, to agree on a baseline leading to peace negotiations. We fully support this aim. To us, it is the right step, which, however, lacks direction. As the saying goes, If you don't know where you're going, any road will lead you there. It was crucial for the European members of the Council— members from the region— to determine the frame accompanying the path to peace at the very outset. To give us a basic direction. And this minimum frame was to determine that peace negotiations should be conducted in line with the principles of the UN Charter. As simple as that. Regional solutions to regional problems apply to all regions. The Security Council members from Europe were compelled to present amendments to the American text. The amendments that mirror the Secretary-General's advice who for 3 years has been underlining that a lasting peace needs to be firmly anchored in the UN Charter and its principles. The amendments that the General Assembly felt necessary to include earlier that morning. The amendments that received 11 votes of the Council members and would have carried in the Security Council were it not for a veto of a country most directly involved in this war. These 2 vetoes were cast in violation of the UN Charter. Mr. President, Europe desperately needs peace, and Slovenia is pleased that the Security Council is finally moving towards its primary task with regard to the war on Ukraine: ensuring a just and lasting peace. Thank you. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Slovenia and now call upon the distinguished representative of South Africa to take the floor.

Mr. President, South Africa appreciates the opportunity to participate in today's debate to consider the use of veto by UN Security Council permanent member in relation to the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. We regret that Russia-Ukraine conflict continues unabated. It is an indictment on the record of the United Nations. In particular the Security Council, which has been unable to exercise its responsibility, that we are not able to realize the consensus on the way forward to bring conflict to an expeditious, peaceful end, despite peace being the core purpose of the organization. Last week in this Assembly, South Africa voted in favor of a resolution tabled on the conflict because: 1, reiterates that the principal purpose of the United Nations, as expressed in the United Nations Charter, is to maintain international peace and security and to peacefully settle disputes. 2, Reaffirm the commitment to the sovereignty, independence, unity, and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders, extending to its territorial waters, and implore a swift end to conflict and further urge a just, lasting, and comprehensive peace between Ukraine and Russia in line with UN Charter and the principle of sovereignty, equality, and territorial integrity of states. I wish to once again emphasize that South Africa remains firmly committed to the need for a peaceful and negotiated resolution to conflict. Within a rule-based system centered on international law, including the principle of UN Charter. South Africa therefore continues to support all efforts to bring the conflict to an end and welcome all measures undertaken thus far in an attempt to kickstart negotiations and bring about lasting peace. We remain steadfast in our commitment to peaceful resolution to conflict through an inclusive and a transparent peaceful process that will lead to a negotiated peaceful and sustainable settlement. Mr. President, South Africa remains concerned at inability of the UN Security Council to to act in unison, which continues to pose a stumbling block to the progressive realization of peace. The lack of meaningful action has resulted in perpetual paralysis of the Council, which impacts on the effectiveness and integrity of the organ. Increasing use of veto highlights the need for reform of the UN Security Council. It is without doubt that the use of veto continues to erode the legitimacy of the Council. We must take concrete steps to ensure that the Council becomes more representative, effective, transparent, and accountable. Addressing the question of veto is central to the discussions on a comprehensive reform of of the Security Council. In conclusion, South Africa reiterates the importance to make real and meaningful progress towards peace rather than contribute towards further divisiveness. We reaffirm our position that the parties to the current conflict should begin to identify areas of common interest in a spirit of compromise and flexibility rather than to continue to fight and firmly hold on their divergent views. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of South Africa. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Chile.

Mr. President, we're grateful for the convening of this plenary session of the General Assembly to discuss the vetoes that took place on the 24th of February, last Monday, in a session convened by the Security Council. Thank you, Mr. President. under the item Maintenance of International Peace and Security in Ukraine. After— 3 years after the beginning of the Russian invasion of Ukraine, we reaffirm our commitment to the respect for the UN Charter, international law, peaceful means of resolving conflicts, and the fundamental principles that govern relations among states. We also would like to make an appeal for an urgent reform of the Security Council. Which— so that it can fulfill its mandate in ensuring international peace and security. Bearing this in mind, Chile repeats its position regarding the use of the veto and the danger that it implies in eroding the credibility and the effectiveness of the multilateral system. We believe that the protection of human life should be our utmost priority and that the use of the veto should be limited. This veto should not be used in circumstances such as mass atrocities and war crimes, as expressed in the French and Mexican initiative and the Code of Conduct for the Response of the Security Council in Cases of Genocide, Crimes Against Humanity, and War Crimes. Both of these mechanisms have the full support of my country. Mr. President, Chile, as a country committed to democracy, human rights, and multilateralism, believes that it is necessary to reform the Security Council so that it is more representative of the diversity of the international community and so that it can tackle more effectively the complexity of new global challenges. It is urgent to eliminate or to at least restrict the use of the veto so that we can guarantee that the decisions of the Council reflect the collective interest rather than the particular interest of the few. Mr. President, Chile, as a founding member of the United Nations and faithful to upholding the Charter and international law, reiterates its commitment to the sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of Ukraine. Resolution 3314 of the General Assembly of 1974 defines aggression and determines that a war of aggression is a crime against international peace. We'd like to reiterate our position regarding the use of the veto and how harmful it is for the legitimacy and credibility of the multilateral system. We will continue to state that the veto is an international responsibility rather than a privilege. Lastly, Mr. President, we'd like to stress that we cannot allow for a world where power is the only argument. We must continue to promote the principle of indivisibility of international security, where the size of a state does not matter. We all have a duty to preserve peace, and with this in mind, security is a shared responsibility to confront the growing threats to the peace— to the peace and security architecture. This is our common duty. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Chile, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of France.

France is actively involved in favor of peace in Ukraine. There can be no lasting peace without respect for the principles that are the very foundation of our collective security. And among these principles is the sovereign equality of states and respect for territorial integrity. To forget these principles is to accept a world where the law of the jungle prevails, where might prevails over right.
