One of these amendments sought to reaffirm the attachment of the Council to the sovereignty, independence, the unity and territorial integrity of Ukraine. Another amendment sought to appeal for a global, just, and lasting peace in line with the principles of the United Nations Charter. Mr. President, in introducing these amendments, we urged the Council to follow the example of the General Assembly, which that very morning adopted similar amendments. These 2 amendments had respectively 9 and 11 favorable votes, votes in favor of them, which should have allowed for their adoption and demonstrated a broad consensus. These amendments recalled the principles of the Charter to which all the UN members are attached. Their adoption should have been self-evident. Self-evident. However, Russia decided alone to use its veto on these essential messages and principles, and this for the simple reason that it is trampling on these principles in Ukraine as an aggressor state. And Russia once again prevented the Security Council from fulfilling its role and affirming its attachment to a respectful Thank you. The Security Council is committed to peace and respect for the principles of the Charter. France deplores this abuse by Russia of its right to veto. We consider that the veto is not a privilege, but a particular responsibility that should be exercised with the goal of allowing the Security Council to act in favor of peace and international security for a just peace and conformity with the Charter. February. The Security Council did not live up to the challenge facing it by adopting a resolution that left out the respect for the Charter and its principles, even while the General Assembly had reaffirmed twice these principles just a few hours ago. Once again, it was the General Assembly, a universal body, which was able to show the way by reaffirming respect for law and solidarity with victims, equality of states, defense of the foundation of the international order and the Charter. France will continue to be mobilized together with its partners to defend the demand for a just and lasting peace that respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine and guarantees the security of the European continent and preserves the principles of the UN Charter. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of France. And I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Greece.

Mr. President, we would like to thank you for convening this plenary meeting on the use of the veto following the veto cast by Russia, a permanent member of the Security Council, on February 24th. Under the agenda item entitled Maintenance of Peace and Security of Ukraine, Greece aligns itself with the statement delivered earlier by the European Union and wishes to add the following remarks in its national capacity. Mr. President, Greece regrets that on February 24th, the Security Council failed to accept amendments to the Resolution Path to Peace which was subsequently adopted as initially drafted in the same meeting. All the more since 2 of the 5 amendments proposed by Member States on that occasion actually secured the necessary number of votes to pass in the Security Council. In a time where the principles of the UN Charter are profoundly challenged in a number of international crises, this latest use of the veto on behalf of a permanent member of the Security Council, and in this particular context, weakens the message we should all be sending. This message is the respect we all owe to international law and the UN Charter as its instrument, which codifies the major principles of international relations, from sovereign equality of states to the prohibition of the use of force. Mr. President, 80 years ago, the UN Charter entrusted the Security Council with a unique mission and ultimate responsibility to maintain peace and security and to enact the prohibition of the use or the threat of use of force around the world. On last week's adoption, in keeping with its responsibility as a member of the Security Council, Greece proposed, along with other UN Security Council members, amendments requesting, among others, a just and lasting peace in this country in line with the UN Charter and its principles. Unfortunately, these amendments were not retained. We note that the General Assembly merely a few hours earlier had spoken with a clear voice on the same subject. adopting all 3 amendments in favor of a just and lasting peace based on the UN Charter principles. Mr. President, Greece has consistently been an ardent supporter of peace. The time of peace in Ukraine has come, but what is needed is not only an end of hostilities, but a just, comprehensive, and lasting settlement through inclusive diplomacy, based on the UN Charter and international law. We need to draw the right lessons and endow any future peace settlement with credible security guarantees for Ukraine that will deter and prevent the recurrence of war in the future. Ukraine is not a regional issue. It has a direct impact on global security and peace. It concerns us all in this Assembly. Ukraine, Europe, indeed the world, need a fair, viable, and thus a lasting peace for Ukraine. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Greece, and I now call on the distinguished representative of Germany to take the floor.

Mr. President, Germany aligns itself with the statements delivered by the European Union and by Liechtenstein on behalf of a group of countries. I want to start by thanking the President of the General Assembly for convening this important meeting. Last week, and here I would like to recall what has happened. The European members of the Security Council, in consultation with Ukraine, proposed 3 draft amendments to a resolution that was just introduced to the Security Council. These amendments were based on crucial elements of 2 resolutions that only hours before the General Assembly had adopted with overwhelming majority. These amendments called for peace negotiations to be conducted within the framework of the United Nations Charter. They made clear that a sham peace, one that does not respect the principles of our Charter, will not endure. The Russian Federation, a member— a permanent member of the Security Council, decided to vote against these amendments, resulting in the use of the veto against 2 out of the 3 amendments. Through the use of the veto, Russia has once again proven a blatant disregard for the sovereignty and the territorial integrity of Ukraine. The vetoes also demonstrated, yet again, Russia's obstinate resistance to the call for a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in line with the UN Charter. The 3 votes of Russia against the amendments also disregarded Article 27, Para 3 of the Charter, which provides that, I quote, In decisions under Chapter VI, a party to a dispute shall abstain from voting. Mr. President, last week this Assembly sent a strong message. It was a message of support for the European amendments. This Assembly stated loud and clear its expectation to achieve a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, a peace rooted in the UN Charter, a peace that respects the sovereignty, the independence, and the territorial integrity of all member states, be they large or be they small. Germany is grateful for the broad support to these principles that has been expressed by members of this Assembly. However, through the vetoes, Russia yet again decided to ignore this appeal, and here I repeat myself, this is the appeal of the broad majority of this Assembly. Last year— last week also clearly demonstrated that the General Assembly's voice in matters of peace and security is indispensable, particularly in situations where one permanent member holds the Council hostage by pursuing its own agenda of territorial conquest and expansionism against a sovereign, independent state and neighbor. Mr. President, Germany welcomes the intention of the resolution put forward by the United States, which was subsequently adopted by the Security Council— the intention to build a momentum towards peace. Together with the 2 resolutions that were adopted by the General Assembly, this strengthens our resolve to finding a lasting solution for peace in Ukraine. We should let this shared ambition guide our collective efforts to bring to an end to this war. And yet the terms of an end to this war can only be decided by negotiations that include Ukraine. No peace will become comprehensive and no peace will be sustainable without Ukraine Ukraine's participation and without Ukraine's consent. Time and again, this Assembly has echoed the resounding call for regional solutions to regional problems. This is exactly what we are working on. It is our strong conviction as Europeans that there can be no peace in Europe without Europe's participation. Germany remains committed to supporting all efforts to achieve a just inclusive, and lasting peace in line with UN Charter, a peace that ensures a safer world for all of us, but above all for the Ukrainian people. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Germany. Thank you, sir. And I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Egypt.

Thank you very much, Mr. President. Mr. President, we meet today as the Russian-Ukrainian crisis enters its 3rd year. You are not without knowing that this crisis does not only affect the parties to the conflict or their regional neighbors, but it also casts a negative shadow on the Global South mainly African states. Egypt was at the heart of these challenges. It was directly affected by the turmoil impacted— impacting food security, supply chains, increases in energy prices as the main importer of grain in the world. At a time when Egypt is shouldering additional burdens for hosting refugees from neighboring countries going through unrest. For this reason, Egypt believes that every war comes to an end, and the voices of reason have an additional responsibility in times of conflict. They have to continue firmly calling for an end to the fighting and putting reason and wisdom first. Egypt engaged in every effort seeking to achieve this goal, whether through an initiative a movement or a draft resolution. Egypt effectively participated in efforts to reach a settlement to the crisis, including the efforts of the Arab Ministerial Contact Group of June 2022, the initiative of African leaders who visited Kyiv and Moscow in July 2023, and lastly, as a founding member of the Friends for Peace Group, which was launched in or established in September 2024 at the initiative of China and Brazil. Now more than ever, it is high time to engage in genuine and real efforts to reach a lasting settlement to the current crisis, to achieve peace and shield the developed and developing worlds from the grave repercussions of a crisis. This size. We welcome the current communication between Russia and the United States and the U.S.-Russian leadership initiative to resolve the situation. It is important to continue making international efforts and build upon them to promote coordination and understanding and make international relations more stable, paving the way towards a lasting and comprehensive solution to the Ukrainian-Russian crisis that addresses its roots causes and ensures it is not repeated. This requires giving the necessary time for a rapprochement and ensuring a conducive environment for its success. Allow me to present the determining factors of the Egyptian position regarding the crisis. They reflect Egypt's firm and principled position regarding all issues, regardless of their context or their geographical location. 1. Lasting solutions for conflicts should be based on the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, the principles of international law, including dialogue and peaceful settlement of disputes. 2. A lasting settlement to the conflict cannot be reached without addressing the root causes of crises and the legitimate security concerns of states which led to the conflict and turned it into a military confrontation, because disregarding this proves an incomplete understanding of the crisis and affects the ability to hold the parties accountable. 3, it is important to maintain and promote effective diplomatic channels to ensure de-escalation. It is also important to refrain from using different tools to fuel the conflict and deepen the polarization such as using economic sanctions. It is also important to stop hostile statements and media campaigns by the parties against each other because they only fuel hatred. 4, it is important to avoid double standards when dealing with current conflicts, current international conflicts. It is not right to call for the respect of the principles of the UN Charter, international law, and international legitimacy in the case of the Ukraine-Russia crisis while disregarding these very same principles in the case of the Palestinian question by way of example. In conclusion, Mr. President, we reaffirm Egypt's full readiness to engage in all genuine efforts to settle the crisis because we are one of the most affected states by this crisis and we have the biggest— one of the biggest interests in making it end. Thank you very much. Shukran.

Mr. President, Excellencies, Poland aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union. We gather today to address the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the largest and longest act of aggression in Europe since the Second World War, actively supported by Belarus. This situation has been recently exacerbated by actions within the UN Security Council. While Resolution 2774 on peace in Ukraine was ultimately adopted, its potential impact was significantly undermined by Russia's decision to twice veto the proposed amendments. These amendments sought to reinforce crucial principles of sovereignty, independence, unity, and territorial integrity of Ukraine. What makes Russia's vetoes even more egregious is the fact that the very same amendments were adopted by a clear majority of the UN membership in the General Assembly the same day. Russia, therefore, not only undermined the Security Council, but effectively silence the voice of the more representative international community. As a result, Russia effectively blocked the call for a just, lasting, and comprehensive peace in line with the UN Charter and the Helsinki Final Act. Such a peace can only be achieved by acknowledging the reality on the ground— that there is an aggressor and a victim. There is no space for a grey zone. Nor can true peace be built on ambiguity. Mr. President, the peace settlement must be more than a mere pause in the conflict that would allow Russia time to rearm and launch another attack. History has shown us this all too many times. A lasting peace agreement must be built upon several fundamental principles. First, it must guarantee the protection of Ukraine's independence, territorial integrity and sovereignty. Second, it must include robust security guarantees for Ukraine to minimize the risk of any renewed Russian aggression. And third, full accountability must be ensured, holding both Russia as a state and the individual perpetrators responsible for all international crimes committed on Ukraine territory or against it. It goes without saying that negotiations cannot be conducted under the duress of bombardment, missile attacks, or nuclear blackmail. In addition, any viable peace proposals or settlements require the assent of Ukraine. Poland aligns itself with this very principle alongside many other like-minded countries. In conclusion, Mr. President, allow me to reiterate that a security Architecture founded on the violation of international law will protect no one. On Monday, a Russian colleague was kind enough to share his knowledge of Polish proverbs here. Quite impressive. In the same spirit of cross-cultural exchange, I may offer this Russian gem: "Sto pasiejesz, to je pasnieś." Our decisions now. especially concerning the upholding of international law and the commitment to achieving sustainable and lasting peace, will determine the long-term stability and prosperity. A reckless course risks a bitter harvest for generations to come. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Poland, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative

Thank you, Mr. President. Ukraine has aligned with the statements delivered by European Union and Liechtenstein on behalf of the group of the UN member states, and we would like to add a few remarks in our national capacity. As an initial co-sponsor of Resolution 76/2, 262 that established the standing mechanism and thus strengthened the role of the General Assembly in a situation when a veto is cast in the Security Council, Ukraine welcomes the fact that this initiative became a vital part in our working practices. The issue of the use of veto has always been of particular importance for Ukraine and those member states who uphold the Charter of the United Nations and its principles. The Russian Federation's behavior in the Council following its aggression against Ukraine is the most vivid example of how detrimental the misuse of veto could be for the Council's capacities to respond effectively to threats to peace and acts of aggression. All draft resolutions that the UN Security Council attempted to adopt in response to the Russian aggression against Ukraine since 2014 2024 were vetoed by the Russian Federation, in particular draft resolutions on condemnation of the Russian Federation's aggression against Ukraine and attempted annexation of the sovereign territories of Ukraine. The most recent case of Russia's veto took place on 24 February when the Security Council considered amendments to UNSC Resolution 2774. These amendments proposed by the Security Council members Denmark, France, Greece, Slovenia, and the United Kingdom would have contributed to bringing the text of this resolution in line with the Charter of the United Nations and reaffirming the commitment to Ukraine's sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders. As a result, the adopted UN Security Council Resolution 2774 lacks essential elements, particularly the classification of the war as an act of aggression by one member state against another. It fails to fully reflect the principles enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations. Thus, the Russian Federation abuses its veto rights either to block the Security Council decision designed to address its aggression, or, as we have seen recently, block those proposals that contribute to just and lasting peace in Ukraine in line with the UN Charter. Particularly noteworthy that the voting in the Security Council was preceded by the General Assembly adoption of the resolution advancing comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine that conveyed a clear, resolute stance of the international community, as well as adoption of the very same amendments. However, this position was not adequately adequately reflected in the Security Council. Mr. President, Ukraine remains a firm supporter of existing initiatives aiming at limiting the use of veto and strengthening the responsibility of its cast, notably the Code of Conduct Regarding Security Council Action Against Genocide, Crimes Against Humanity, or War Crimes prepared by the ACT Group, as well as Franco-Mexican initiative on the suspension We should not tolerate ongoing ignorance of the principle contained in Article 27 of the UN Charter, envisaging that in decisions under Chapter VI and under paragraph 3 of Article 52, a party to a dispute shall abstain from voting. This is an important tool to prevent immobilization of the Security Council since the early stages of situation of concern. Thank you. The use of the veto should also be restricted when a permanent member is directly involved in the conflict under consideration of the Council and therefore cannot be expected to exercise its voting rights and privileges in an impartial manner. We encourage the General Assembly to continue exploring ways of further improvement of the Assembly's toolbox and ability to help the Security Council in case of casting vetoes. We encourage those member states that have not yet joined the, the veto initiatives to do so. Mr. President, nobody wants peace more than Ukrainians. But peace must be real, not just a word. It must be just, reliable, and lasting. And this can only be achieved through strong and long-term security guarantees for Ukraine, Europe, and the entire world. I thank you. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ukraine, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ecuador.

Mr. President, February during the consideration of 2 oral amendments to the text that was adopted as Resolution 2774. As has been mentioned by various colleagues already, the proposed amendments that were vetoed in the Council on the afternoon of the 24th of February repeated literally word for word the text of the amendments adopted just a few hours before that by this same Assembly with a vote in favor of 93 countries. Consequently, it's a fact that the veto by one of the countries to which the Charter has granted this right or privilege ignored the position of the majority in this Assembly. Mr. President, the Charter contains provisions that unfortunately are often disregarded. Respect for the provisions of the Charter should be comprehensive. It is not acceptable to choose those articles that are convenient and to leave out or not respect those that are determined to be contrary to one's interest. Thus, the application in good faith of paragraph 3 of Article 27 of the Charter should be the first step toward the reform of the Security Council that we have been discussing for so long. The application in good faith of this article does not require any change in the text of the Charter. It requires no conferences. It requires no meetings or voting. The only thing it requires is a genuine commitment to the Charter. Mr. President, colleagues, Ecuador has participated in all the sessions convened by the Assembly to discuss the use of the veto because we are convinced that these debates serve as a magnifying glass for the arguments of those states whose positions differ from the country that used the veto and which clearly demonstrate, as is the— in this case, the divergence between the majority opinion of the membership and the sole, the single position of one of the members of the Council. Since starting with the negotiations before the signature of the Charter 80 years ago, Ecuador has consider the veto as an anti-democratic privilege, and we've always been opposed to it. It should be recalled, however, that the— it is true that the power of the veto could have been used to avoid a situation where the majority opinion of the General Assembly is ignored, which is a responsibility that also falls on those who have the right to cast a veto. Lastly, Mr. President, Ecuador would like to reiterate its conviction that the mechanism established by Resolution 76/262 contributes to transparency and accountability and thus bolsters the authority of the General Assembly and its relationship with the Council and consequently strengthens Thank you very much. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ecuador and now call on the distinguished representative of Czechia.

Mr. President, Czechia aligns itself with the statement delivered by the European Union, and now allow me to deliver a few remarks in my national capacity. Czechia welcomes this opportunity to address the recent use of the veto and the United Nations Security Council. The veto power granted to the permanent members of the Security Council by the international community should be exercised only in extraordinary circumstances and with clear justification. Such prudent use of the veto ensures that the Council's decisions command broad support and legitimacy across the global community. However, last week we witnessed a stark contrast between the General Assembly's unequivocal condemnation of Russia's war of aggression and its call for a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in Ukraine based on the UN Charter on the one hand, and the subsequent action in the Security Council on the other. In the Security Council, Russia twice cast its veto during the adoption of the Path to Peace resolution, leaving no doubt about its true intentions for peace in Ukraine. First, Russia vetoed a simple reaffirmation of its commitment to the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders. And then it vetoed a call for a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in accordance with the UN Charter and the principles of sovereign equality and territorial integrity of states. By vetoing these fundamental principles, of our multilateral system, Russia, a permanent member of the Security Council, has once again blatantly demonstrated that it has no interest in respecting the rules of peaceful coexistence among nations enshrined in the UN Charter and international law. And this is why we insist that how we establish the terms of peace in Ukraine remains of paramount importance. Because the aggressor has repeatedly rejected peace in accordance with international law. Moscow has consistently demanded Ukraine's capitulation while pursuing its total subjugation. History has shown that Russia will not stop halfway. And the only thing that can stop it is our unified support for Ukraine. Mr. President, the war in Ukraine is a struggle for fundamental principles. We all want to live in a world founded on mutual respect and dialogue, where international law prevails. Not one determined by aggression and heavy-handed bullying. Czechia remains firmly committed to supporting Ukraine's desire for peace. What we need and strive for is a durable peace grounded in the principles of the UN Charter, one that will stand the test of time rather than merely providing the aggressor with an opportunity to reconstitute its, its forces and resume its campaign of territorial conquest. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Czechia, and I call— now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Japan.

Thank you, Mr. President. 3 years have passed since Russia began its unprovoked war of aggression against the sovereign nation of Ukraine. It is quite regrettable that Russia has disregarded the repeated calls from the members of the General Assembly and the entire international community. The consequences of Russia's ruthless and indiscriminate attacks have been significant, with tremendous losses of life and injuries to innocent civilians, and the global repercussions are far-reaching. Japan condemns in strongest terms Russia's aggression against Ukraine and hopes that the various diplomatic efforts which are currently ongoing will bear fruit and help achieve a breakthrough in the situation. Mr. President, the UN Charter serves as the foundation of all international relations and a common agreement that all member states must faithfully observe. It is particularly crucial for a permanent member who is supposed to bear the heaviest burden for the maintenance of international peace and security under Article 1, Paragraph 1 of its Charter to fulfill its special responsibility. Russia's aggression against Ukraine is, however, a clear and blatant violation of international law, including the UN Charter, fundamentally undermining the foundation. If such violations were to be ignored, it would send the international community back to a state of chaos, driven by brute force and coercion. We therefore stand side by side with the people of Ukraine. We must uphold the international order based on the rule of law. Japan aspires diplomatic efforts under the solidarity of international community will lead to a realization of a just and lasting peace based on the purposes and principles of the UN Charter as soon as possible. Furthermore, as decided in the Pact for the Future, Japan believes that we need to fully implement and adhere all provisions of the Charter of the United Nations as they relate to the decision-making process in Security Council, including Article 27 of the Charter. Japan also strongly condemns the engagement of North Korea's troops in combat against Ukraine, which also constitutes a clear violation of international law, including the UN Charter. Japan also reiterates its deep concern about the military cooperation between Iran and Russia. The international community refrains from any action Direct or indirect, that would support Russia's aggression. Japan reiterates that this is not a matter of choosing sides between Ukraine and Russia, but a matter of principle of either upholding or disregarding the UN Charter. Any unilateral attempt to change the status quo by force is unacceptable anywhere in the world. and such an attempt should never succeed. The repercussions of allowing such attempts to occur would, would be global and undoubtedly affect everyone for years to come. Mr. President, Japan reiterates its deepest respect and unwavering solidarity with the people of Ukraine, who have been defending their country and its future for for 3 long years. Japan will continue its support, its efforts, and stand firmly with Ukraine and the international community until comprehensive, just, and lasting peace based on the purposes and principles of the UN Charter is achieved in Ukraine. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Japan. And I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Spain.

Thank you, Mr. President. Spain would like to align itself with the statement made by the European Union and Liechtenstein and would like to make some additional comments that our national Promotes the elimination of the veto. We are grateful to Denmark, Greece, France, Slovenia, and the United Kingdom for introducing the 3 amendments to the draft resolution presented in the Council. These amendments were aimed at situating the appeal to put an end to the Russian aggression against Ukraine in its proper context. We all share this goal, in line with the 2 resolutions approved by the General Assembly in the morning of the 24th of February. The search for a just and lasting peace should be in compliance with the UN Charter and the principles of sovereign equality and territorial integrity of states. Spain condemns in the strongest terms the Russian aggression against Ukraine, which is contrary to the most basic principles of international law and the UN Charter. Lastly, we reiterate that the search for a lasting and just peace must include the participation of Europe and first and foremost the participation of Ukraine as a country that was attacked, ensuring the respect for its independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Spain and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Denmark.

Thank you, Mr. President. Denmark aligns itself with the statement made by Iceland on behalf of the Nordic countries, the European Union on behalf of the EU and its member states, and Liechtenstein on behalf of a group of countries. Denmark is a strong supporter of the Veto Initiative. We firmly believe that peace and security is a collective effort of the United Nations. Thank you. When the Security Council fails, the General Assembly must step in. We welcome the transparency and accountability offered by today's meeting. Mr. President, we are meeting today to listen to the Russian Federation's explanation for using its veto twice in the Security Council on the 3rd anniversary of its brutal, full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Let us recall that It is Russian airstrikes overnight that have again brought more death, destruction, and misery to the civilian population in Ukraine, including a ballistic missile hitting a hotel in Kyiv with, with at least 4 deaths. But nothing we have heard today could justify vetoing basic references to the UN Charter and fundamental principles of international law. 2 vetoes cast against such sovereignty and territorial integrity by a permanent member that has invaded its neighbor and ever since used its P5 status to evade accountability. A more brazen abuse of power in the UN system is hard to imagine. The use of the veto by a permanent member which is a party to the dispute is limited by paragraph 27 of the Charter. The identification of the Russian Federation as a party is in the first paragraph of their best adapted resolution, so it is crystal clear. Mr. President, let us not forget that the amendments the Russian Federation chose to veto were supported by the majority of Council members. And let us also keep in mind that just hours before the vote in the Security Council, the vast majority of members President Vosink in this assembly chose to stand with Ukraine and the UN Charter. They rejected the false equivalence between aggressor and victim. They reaffirmed their commitment to Ukraine's sovereignty and territorial integrity. They supported a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace in line with the UN Charter. In doing so, they also showed solidarity with the people of Ukraine. A people who have been the victim of tremendous human suffering. A people whose much larger neighbor, Russia, began a campaign to change internationally recognized borders by force. Let us remember, if Russia stops fighting, the war will end. If Ukraine stops fighting, It will cease to exist as an independent country. Russia's war and aggression has caused thousands of civilian casualties and humanitarian stress. Millions more have been displaced, both within Ukraine's borders and beyond. Almost 13 million people in Ukraine need humanitarian assistance due to Russia's blatant violation of the UN Charter. Let there be no doubt. Denmark welcomes genuine efforts to end this senseless war and for the Security Council to act in accordance with its responsibilities. But peace must be on the right terms. We must not reward the aggressor. We must adhere to the founding principles of the UN system as enshrined by the UN Charter and applicable under international law. For all states, large and small, the Charter is the promise that their sovereignty, territorial integrity, and political independence will be protected, that the world does not again turn into a place where might is right. Denmark entered the Security Council with a promise to stand up for international law. We intend to keep that promise. Mr. President, let me conclude by stressing that Denmark stands with the people of Ukraine. We'll support you and your freedom as long as it takes. As we saw last week, so does the vast majority of the international community that voted in the General Assembly. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Denmark and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ireland.

President, Ireland aligns itself with the statement of the European Union. On the morning of the 24th of February, on the 3rd anniversary of Russia's illegal and unprovoked full-scale invasion of Ukraine, this Assembly adopted 2 very significant resolutions. These resolutions reaffirmed the UN General Assembly's steadfast commitment to international law and the fundamental principle of respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states. These resolutions acknowledged Russia's unacceptable and illegal aggression against Ukraine and demanded accountability from the aggressor state. And these resolutions outlined the basis for a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, an approach to peace now adopted by the General Assembly, with enduring respect for the principles and purposes of the UN Charter at its core. This was a vitally important message that we, as member states, sent to the world on that anniversary, and one that resonates far beyond Ukraine and Europe. The General Assembly made clear that morning that the cause of Ukraine is not a cause of West, of North and South, or East and West. It is the cause of right versus wrong, It is a matter of order and principle. That principle, that orders— that borders cannot be changed by force, protects us all. It must apply equally across the world, from Africa to the Middle East, and from Europe to Asia and the Americas, without exception. President, in the face of overlapping crises and increasing polarisation, the adoption of these resolutions also demonstrated the enduring commitment of member states to these core values in very challenging times. These are universal values that apply to each of us equally and in full. Any credible future for multilateralism depends on them. We regret that in the afternoon of that same day, the Russian Federation used the unjustifiable power of the veto to twice block the Security Council from endorsing the same principles and values in proposed amendments. That the Security Council was prevented by Russia in urging a just, last, and comprehensive peace between Ukraine and Russia in line with the UN Charter demonstrates the problem that we face: the fact that Russia does not want peace. That the Security Council was also blocked by Russia in reaffirming the Council's commitment to the sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders makes all of us less secure— all of us. President, we welcome and commend genuine efforts to bring about an end to this brutal war, and we thank the United States for its commitment to advance peace for Ukraine. Resolution 2774 represents an important first gesture by the Security Council, but it is not sufficient. The unjust power of the veto has left the resolution bereft of the essential commitments— the essential commitments that must underpin a just and lasting peace. It has allowed the aggressor to deny the Council its genuine expression of the facts of the matter. It is our duty to make clear those facts today. Many of us have known conflict in our past. We understand the true value of peace and have travelled a long and difficult road to building it— the value of real peace, the value of true peace. And we know that any end to conflict without justice will not bring a peace that lasts, a peace that endures. The decisions of our shared institutions of international justice reinforce the collective condemnation that we as UN member states have made of Russia's reprehensible aggression against Ukraine. These decisions must guide us as we seek to craft a peace in line with the UN Charter and international law. They promise a peace founded on justice, the only peace that can last. And it must be an inclusive peace. Ukraine and Europe must be central to any process and must determine the timing and terms of any agreement. President, nobody wants peace more than Ukraine and the Ukrainian people, and nobody has made a greater sacrifice for that peace than the Ukrainian people themselves. Ukraine deserves the same right that we all claim to determine our own future in peace, in dignity, and in security. This Assembly has now agreed on 8 occasions, in 9 separate resolutions, how to deliver that peaceful future, one founded on upholding the UN Charter. And in the face of the aggressor's veto, we clearly assert today, as the General Assembly, our demand to realize that true path to peace. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Sierra Leone.

Mr. President, I thank the President of the General Assembly for convening this meeting as mandated by Resolution 76/262 adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in 2022 and following the exercise of the veto by a permanent member in the Security Council. We believe that this debate provides member states with a valuable opportunity to consider the impact of the veto on the functioning and effectiveness of the Security Council in fulfilling its mandate as it relates to the lives and livelihoods of peoples and relevant country situations. At the meeting held on the 24th of February, 2025, the Security Council took action and adopted Resolution 2774 under the agenda item Maintenance of Peace and security of Ukraine. Sierra Leone voted in favor of the resolution, and our votes on the respective amendment were guided by the principal position that the UN should help foster peace between nations and that Ukraine must be at the forefront of any peace process or agreement in accordance with the principles of the UN Charter. Additionally, the legitimate concerns of all parties must be addressed. During the Council's briefing under the same agenda item held on the same day, we elaborated on our position on the issue, and that is the urgent need for cessation of hostilities in the Ukraine conflict and an end to the immense suffering of civilians caught on both sides of this conflict. Mr. President, we are convened today, and both organs of the UN, the General Assembly in the 11th Emergency Special Session and the Security Council, met under the shadow of a conflict that challenges the very foundation of our international rules-based system. In doing so, Let me recall a guiding principle reiterated by the President of Poland during his address to this Assembly on 4 March: peace through law. This simple yet profound phrase underlines that true and lasting peace is achieved not by the force of arms, but by the force of law. By respect for the Charter of the UN and the whole body of international law, we endorse this vision. Peace through law means that no nation is above the rules that bind us all. It is in that spirit that we view the veto initiative, the new General Assembly mechanism to scrutinize any use of the veto, as a valuable tool rooted in the supremacy of the law and accountability. When the Security Council cannot act because of a veto, the wider membership of the UN, upholding our legal and moral principles, must have its voice heard. This is multilateralism at work, ensuring that might does not mean right. Mr. President, Sierra Leone's own history and commitment to peace compels us to stand firmly on the side of international law. In the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, my delegation's vote and statement have been consistent with the UN Charter principles and the obligation to settle disputes by peaceful means. We participated in the emergency special session on Ukraine and voted in favor of the General Assembly resolutions addressing that conflict. These resolutions, which Sierra Leone supported, reaffirmed the Charter. They uphold the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine, reject the unlawful use of force, and call for the peaceful resolution of the dispute. They demand an immediate cessation of hostilities, and a return to dialogue in line with international law. By voting for this text, Sierra Leone made clear that our position is principled. We are guided by the consistent application of international law, for it is only through such consistency that we can maintain a rules-based system that protects all states, big and small. Mr. President, we also acknowledge efforts in the Security Council to address the conflict in Ukraine. We further acknowledge the recent initiative by the United States in the Council to table a sunset resolution aimed at finding a path towards peace. That text implores a swift end to the conflict and urges a lasting peace between Ukraine and the Russian Federation, encapsulating the very objectives of the United Nations Charter. In essence, it asks for nothing beyond what we all seek: an end to violence and the start of dialogue. Sierra Leone welcomes the focus on dialogue and diplomacy. We view it as a reaffirmation that even the Security Council, despite divisions, can rally around fundamental Charter aims when the language is centered on humanitarian and peace imperatives. It is regretful, however, that the Council has often been paralyzed by the use of the veto. This brings me to the broader issue of the veto power. and the urgent need for reform. Sierra Leone hereby asserts the common African position on Security Council reform as espoused in the Ezoumeni Consensus and SIT Declaration. Africa's position is clear: we fundamentally oppose the continued existence of the veto in its current form, for it contradicts the very principle of sovereign equality enshrined in the UN Charter. The veto is the most undemocratic element of our UN architecture, often undermining the collective security interests of the wider membership. We believe that abolishing the veto will greatly enhance the Security Council's credibility and effectiveness. However, we are also pragmatic. As long as the veto exists, it must not privilege the few. It should be extended to all new permanent members in a reformed Council as a matter of common justice and equality. The status quo, where Africa comprising 54 UN Member States has no permanent seat and no voice in veto decisions, is a historical injustice. that must be rectified. Sierra Leone, as one of the African states on the Council, carries a mandate to advocate for these reforms. We will lend our voice to calls for a more democratic Security Council that reflects today's world and curtails the misuse of the veto. In the interim, we note the utility of the veto initiative in the General Assembly which brings transparency and accountability whenever a veto is cast, as another important step in the right direction. It ensures that the Council's deadlock does not mean the world's silent. Law, we assert, must reign supreme over power politics. Let me therefore conclude by reaffirming Sierra Leone's commitment to peace through law. We call for the immediate cessation of hostilities as good faith towards dialogue. I thank you.

A large number of NGOs as well as other stakeholders from Türkiye have already been contributing to all spheres of work of the UN and working together with the UN all over the globe, in particular in most vulnerable countries. We believe that the criteria and principles formulated in ECOSOC Resolution 1996/31 should apply to all NGOs who seek to participate in the conferences and meetings of the UN. We believe that participation of NGOs in a UN process should be handled in good faith between concerned Member States that may have full information about the activities of the NGOs in question. As a matter of fact, for the purposes of transparency, for an informed decision-making, it is highly important for member states to know in detail how those NGOs and stakeholders plan to contribute to the high-level meeting. As the present resolution has not been amended today, Türkiye disassociates itself from OP9 of the resolution. Thank you.
